title: The Fragile Truce Between the Working Class and the Woke Left
text:
new video loaded: The Fragile Truce Between the Working Class and the Woke Left
transcript
The Fragile Truce Between the Working Class and the Woke Left
Democrats have power now. They shouldn’t waste it on culture wars.
- For New York Times Opinion I’m Christine Rosen, guest hosting for “Interesting Times.” It’s clear the Democrats won this recent election because they ran on the economy. “This win is for every teacher and every nurse, for every farmer and every rancher, for every young person who’s trying to buy a home.” “We promised to fight for an affordable America, and that’s exactly what we will do.” I’m not sure that’s where they’re going to end up, though. I’ve seen the Democratic Party repeatedly fall into the trap of fighting culture wars, focusing on identity politics. Are they really going to care about the working class this time? My guest this week is also skeptical. She’s worried that the Democratic Party could derail this opportunity by focusing too much on what she calls trauma politics. “It’s actually creating a culture war that attacks working-class people. And that’s the thing that really rankles me.” Catherine Liu is a left-wing cultural critic whose most recent book is “Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering.” Catherine Liu, welcome to “Interesting Times.” We’ve just come out of a midterm election, historic transfer of power to the Democratic Party. Are we over identity politics? I’m afraid not. And I think that there is going to be a lot of resistance to its demise. There is too much at stake within the N.G.O. industrial complex to wield trauma as a kind of instrument, a blunt instrument to make elites fall into line. And I wish I could say that we’re heading towards a more objective, more just, more economically oriented politics on the left-liberal side of things, but I’ve been really shocked at how persistent this kind of identitarianism can be. But I think that we’ve turned a corner. What I was really, really heartened by was the kind of warm language that Talarico, Hinojosa and even Abdul El-Sayed were able to use, and they were not lecturing people. This is a very different kind of campaigning. It’s an interesting departure from even just two years ago, 2024, where identity politics, language really dominated a lot of the Democratic Party’s message, and they lost. But I’m curious. I set you up by asking you identity politics, because in fact, you don’t really use that term a lot in your work. You talk about trauma politics and trauma scripts. Thank you for noticing. Well, I’m curious why you have chosen to use that word. What does that mean? What are some distinctions between that and identity politics? Well, so I’m trying to get at the root of why identity politics was embraced by liberals and progressives. And one of the things that I found was that it was a successful strategy to talk about victimhood after the social movements ran out of steam in the ’70s and especially in the ’80s — that it was an attempt to try to make a moral language out of a secular drive to be more to create a more just society. So if we created this category about victimization and social inequity, we could maybe peel some — and I’m saying “we” from the liberal left point of view — peel some of right-wing or the conservatives or the religious people over to our side. And in the end it became like a snowball. It went out of control, partially because it was so successful at framing issues from the top-down. The Democrats, in my lifetime, when I was coming up in the world, in the ’80s, were really trying to grasp at straws about how they had lost the popular appeal. So they appealed to these purely symbolic cultural things that didn’t look at actual economic struggles, economic redistribution, and in fact, since 2016, the Democratic Party elites kind of characterized the working-class man, the working-class white man as the enemy of progress. And I think that was a terrible politics, terrible strategy. And this last election showed incredible diversity of candidates that succeeded, but they succeeded because they were people of principle who happened to be people of color. And that I was very, very heartened by. They didn’t play the people-of-color card first. They were people of principle. That’s interesting. So those of us on the conservative side of the aisle have long critiqued — including myself — have long critiqued what’s called therapy culture. This elevation of victimhood, promotion of fragility, lack of resilience. So this isn’t — a lot of what I read in your work, it wasn’t new to me in that sense. But I come at it from a different perspective. I’m curious, where do you see the trauma politics that you discuss and critique overlapping, fitting in or not, with some of the long standing conservative critique of therapy culture, for example? So the conservatives come out of a long tradition. I mean, not MAGA, but conservative, traditional conservative you for making that distinction. Thank you. Because MAGA maka kind of embraced grievance and therapy and victimhood. But the conservative tradition comes out of a kind of what I think of as being like a sense of the importance of strong boundaries between the personal and the political right. And that was something that feminism wanted to overturn. But this kind of idea of republicanism, small r, had to do with the fact that you took care of your family, your home, your being, your citizenship at home in a very private way. And then you emerge into the public to talk about politics, to debate politics. And therefore, when you had a disagreement, it wasn’t a personal issue. This is a very, very old, stoic tradition that comes out of the ancients, actually. And I think the left liberal side of things went really crazy when they decided that disagreements were all personal and personal attacks. So maybe this is where I fall more on the conservative side of things. And I am not afraid of that. People are like, oh my God, aren’t you afraid you’re going to be construed as right wing. And I think it’s time for us to find common ground. Like if we can find common ground on this, then we can move forward as a country and make clear our disagreements and agreements, but still feel committed to a common project, which is to heal this country because things are very, very askew. I’m just going to use a more vulgar word. But our listeners, thank you for your. Well, I’m at the time, so I’m afraid, but if I were a regular podcast, I would have said the word. But, it’s like the boundaries between public and private were really important for small r republicanism. And that comes out of the Enlightenment. So I’m sorry that it became a conservative point of view because I think this therapeutic language actually dovetailed really nicely with the massive consumerist attitude that women and minorities were encouraged to take about their own experiences, about their own identities. And I think that has been a personal detriment and a public detriment. Well, that personal is political, which all young women grew up hearing of the feminist messaging you just attack straight on at the beginning of your book. And the example you give is one I’m remember being struck by at the time as well, and that was Representative Alexandria ocasio-cortez’s Instagram about January 6, and her experience and her revelation of having been a victim of sexual assault to friends and loved ones close to me. I want to apologize to them in advance. Sorry if my voice is shaking, but if you are learning things about me in the course of this life that you didn’t know before, why did you choose that particular moment to begin your critique of trauma politics. I wanted to bookend this kind of discourse with AOC in the beginning. And Oprah at the end, and just show how this kind of therapy culture is aligned with a kind of neoliberal agenda for self-objectification. It was genuinely disappointing to me because I was on that Ig Live to hear what she had said had to say on two levels, one that she exposed herself to and her great secrets. When she admitted that many people close to her didn’t even know about it. And then because I felt almost a maternal sense of protectiveness about her, she had been the target of so much misogynistic attack, especially from the right. And I was like, O.K, I don’t know why you’re exposing yourself this way to more. I wanted to give her a hug and move her away from her phone. Secondly, though, one of the things I was expecting her to talk about, which I think is one of the most important parts of constitutional liberal democracy as we know it, is the question of peaceful succession. And that was what was shaken on January six. And I was like, I wanted to talk about this. Yes, I thought, this is what’s happened. This is what’s important that’s happening to our country. She has always been an Instagram politician. From day one, she was live streaming, being a Congresswoman for the first time. That’s how she often seems to cultivate her followers more even than her actual bread and butter constituents. She’s gained a huge amount of cultural power from that. So is do you think that it was more that that’s who she is, an Instagram politician, or was it the trauma politics in particular that made that message resonate for so many of her followers. Instagram politics is trauma politics. Social media wants us to adhere to its values, its addictive sense of instant gratification and dopamine. But on the other hand, I have a big social media presence as well, and I don’t think it should has to be that it could be educational. So I thought, this is a unique opportunity for a young politician who’s lived through this, actual physical confrontation with a constitutional crisis that threatens the very ground of liberal democracy if we’re going to believe in it. And she’s using this to confess to this very, very personal and private event in her life. But what Oprah shows is that this kind of thing on broadcast cast media can create more adhesion from your audience. Expand your audience legitimize your brand. Well, it’s interesting you use the word brand because I was going to. I want to ask how you think we got to this moment. So look back over not just the past 10 years, which have been a rather chaotic time in American politics and culture, but further back. What is the reward mechanism that was put in place that encouraged not just our politicians, but celebrities. And now, with the advent of social media, ordinary people to constantly follow a trauma script, to see trauma as a kind of currency for attention. Is this a blip. Or is this something you see, having built over time. We got here because we made poor choices earlier on. I don’t know about poor choices, but the structure of television was really, really transformed when Oprah Winfrey went on TV and confessed to having been a victim of childhood sexual abuse. I was interviewing these people who had been sexually abused, and I didn’t want people to think that I was being exploitive and that I was trying to be sensationalist. She did expand the purview of what we could discuss in public on broadcast media. At the time, and I think that she synthesized the transgressive ethos of the hippies with the entrepreneurialism, self-objectification of yuppies. And at that moment, she was able to transform those two threads of American culture that were producing the 1980s into something that marked her brand forever, legitimized her, differentiated her from Geraldo Rivera, Jerry Springer, Sally Jessy Raphael. And her most immediate competitor at the time was Phil Donahue. Donahue so she really knew how to use the medium of television, because television itself was always seen as somewhat like vulgar, low. Like bad. From the middle brow, high brow cultural elites. And one of the ways that it tried to legitimize itself in the 50s and 60s was that it wanted to make itself informative. So they had a lot of talk shows. The sponsors would come on Lysol or dove, but the selling was marginalized. And the information and the discussion was supposed to model like a Democratic public sphere. By the time you get to daytime television and 24 hour news cycles, you have an increasingly intensive need to sell, inform, and draw your audience into this kind of intimacy that was very unique to the medium. Now, social media has taken on that role. That’s accelerated that trend significantly. Oprah, I think, also had a third strand which appealed to people of a more traditional or conservative sensibility, which was bootstraps, right. She pulled herself up. She liked to tell the story of how she grew up poor and how she made this built this empire for herself. And I’m curious because one of the things you do in your book, again, perhaps a point of agreement for the right and the left today is you talk about how these trauma scripts have become a tool of the professional management class, the elites. So criticism of the elites is now coming from both sides, both sides of the aisle pretty intensely. But what do you mean when you talk about this professional managerial class, and how does it relate to our political culture more broadly. Well they are a class of credentialed experts. I have a PhD. I worked hard to get it. I have a status in the academic world that I feel like I earned after 30 years, and we’re supposed to be somewhat neutral and protected from market forces. What we’ve seen in the past, I don’t 50 years is the deep compromise of this class. Doctors were on the payroll of big pharma. Professors were doing research that favored certain kinds of purposes for big donors. And we trusted these elites during the 1930s to right the ship after the financial crisis. But I would say that this class has become increasingly willing to sacrifice the well-being of the majority of Americans for the profit of the capitalist class, and for its own status as a protector of the status quo. Yes I wanted to clarify that so that our listeners understand this is not just a critique of elite or of the ivory tower. You talk about the capitalist liberal elite. So where does that description fit with the Democratic Party today. Up until the 70s, the Democratic Party was dominated by working class people and unions non-college-educated people, and by 77. They saw the complete takeover of the Democratic Party elite by what conservatives called the New class, the conservatives would. I think Spiro Agnew called them the nattering nabobs of negativity. They had the conservatives were understood that this class was taking power, had and was creating a huge rift between what the Democratic Party had once represented and what it was now going to represent, which you could make a caricature of this Berkeley to Cambridge, the Berkeley to Cambridge continuum. In my very, very wealthy neighborhood in Orange County we see signs in the yard, in this house, we believe in science, in this house, we do this and this. And there’s a lot of posturing that has to do with what I wrote about in virtue hoarders that proclaims, on the consumer side of things, more progressive consumerist practices that average Americans can’t afford. Nobody can afford to shop at Whole Foods unless they’re making $500,000 a year. I mean, I’m just going to say that right now. Well, the family and this is actually I’m glad you mentioned Orange County, home of the country club Republican label. And there is a they’re disappearing. Well, they’re almost gone. And in its place, though, you have a kind of concierge, Democratic Party, people who can afford Whole Foods, who can put those signs in this house, we believe. So I’m curious to push a little bit on why you chose not to frame this as what conservatives have seen as a long standing culture war, culture war, culture war. We see and the argument has long been that New class, those nattering nabobs, weren’t just trying to gain prestige and power. They actually had a brief to undermine traditional American values, to really challenge some of the premises of Western civilization, that this was a real threat, not just an intellectual threat, but a threat to future generations of Americans being raised in an environment where they were taught things that were incorrect. So you again, you’re coming. You’re framing is different. I found it really fascinating. I’m wondering, though, again, if there’s a reason you chose not to pitch this as part of a broader culture war, if you see it as distinct from that, it is part of a larger culture war. But I was trying to look at how they’re waging a symbolic culture war on one hand, but practicing something completely different on the other. So that was my target, because all of to Sociological Studies that have been done by people I really admire Jennifer Silva, have shown that the working class family is completely destroyed in America that if you born into a working class milieu of whatever race, you have more chance of being born out of wedlock than being born to married parents. The rate of divorce is going up in working class circles in America. These people who are preaching, experimentation, all this other stuff, college educated women have a much smaller chance of being divorced right now than ever before. College educated people have very stable relationships. So this is the thing that drives me nuts. It’s like hypocrisy. It seems like a kind of hypocrisy. Hypocrisy but it’s actually creating a culture war that attacks working class people. And that’s what I’m most that that’s the thing that really rankles me now. The country club Republicans of Orange County today are more very wealthy small business people. And they’re much more upstarts. Like, I have a lot of friends who I love who are Republicans. They have experienced extreme class mobility in their lifetimes, but they have not gone to college. And that’s unusual now. Yes yeah. So this is a very interesting configuration for me because even though there are many women who may not who I play tennis with who may not have millions, they have the college credential and that actually determines their political positions. And they feel like they’re really enlightened. But I feel like both sides are completely captured by different forms of propaganda. Well, this actually, this is a good segue into talking a little bit about the midterm voting, because we did see, we’ve seen that the Democratic Party tends to get wealthier, more college educated people. Now, that coalition is almost flipped from people who used to vote for Republicans. But I think the material situation of the average American was what was front and center. The cost of groceries, the cost of gas, the cost of housing. And also a little bit about government corruption. I’ll say from the conservative side of the aisle, it seemed like a rewind back to the 2024 culture war playbook for most of the Republican candidates. A lot of them avoided talking about these economic issues. A few exceptions. I mean, Governor of Florida, Ron DeSantis, after the midterm elections, chastised Republicans. Four years ago, we were in the peak woke era. It alienated a lot of people, rightfully so. It alienated me. So we were fighting back against that. Well, now the issues are different. And Republicans, they really were fighting yesterday’s battles. Who in the most recent elections do you think avoided the trauma trap. The trauma script trap and instead talked about these issues well, while still getting the voters to listen to them, because that is and I want to talk about that in a minute, why this is so appealing to people. I think James Talarico did a great job. I actually think Angie Nixon did a great job. She lost in Florida. I think that Gina Hinojosa did a great job of avoiding culture, war, language and talking about the struggles of Texans. I think that there is a huge anti-authoritarian. Backlash against this kind of condescension that now comes from the right. I mean, I just turned on Fox this morning and Sean Hannity is making fun of Rosie O’Donnell. “Alright, time now for the other news of the day. A major update from Trump-derangement-syndrome patient zero: Rosie is back.” Like he’s talking about something that nobody cares about anymore about how Rosie left the country because she hated Trump. It’s this he’s trying to revive culture wars because it’s the only script he knows and making fun of. Like liberal trauma, liberal snowflakes. Nobody cares about that anymore. Like, everyone should be focused and is focused on the questions of the day, which are economic and which have to do with corruption and just absolute illegality that the Trump administration is performing in defiance of Republican small r values. That should be values that we’re trying to figure out how to instantiate to fight against the oligarchs. He got into bed with the oligarchs. There was something about him being like, I’m against forever wars, and I’m going to drain the swamp that Americans responded to then. And he’s betrayed all of those kinds of promises that he made to actually get rid of corruption and waste. He’s up corruption, waste. So I feel like there is a. Bread and butter issue focus that Mamdani was capable of that Bernie Sanders continued to emphasize. And it sounds so boring to keep talking about bread and butter but bread and butter is a problem right now. And childcare as well. The pronatalist conservatives had no economic plan for how to help young people establish families, take care of children Yeah it was interesting. There was a lot of repeating of plans and encouraging people to have more children. But then when policy came to it and this is policy at a time when the Republicans did control Congress, there wasn’t much movement. I do want to posit a candidate who maybe tried to have it both ways. El-sayed certainly talked a lot about prescription drug pricing. Those were his ads all over Michigan. America is the greatest country in the world and in the richest, most powerful country. It just shouldn’t be this hard to get by. It shouldn’t be this hard to buy groceries to afford health. It’s probably a large part of the reason he won is he was really emphasizing those economic conditions, but he would sit down and do interviews and he would talk about things like speaking truth to pain and people being in their trauma. We talk a lot about truth to power, but I think it’s actually a lot harder to speak truth to pain. And I say that as someone who went to medical school realizing that a lot of our politics right now, we’ve got to get a lot better at speaking truth to pain if we’re going to get through some of these challenges that we have. So is he an example of someone trying to square the circle that you’ve described. So I think a lot of younger people like him, they grew up in this world like it’s hard for them to transition to another language like my colleagues and faculty meetings are like, we’re speaking truth to power. And I’m like, where is the power in this room. We’re trying to get enough resources to teach our students properly, but it’s this default position that he takes on. What I liked about his campaign is that he was combative, and I feel like a lot of Democratic politicians, they look like up until this year they were made in a vat, they were cloned. And I feel like there’s a place for spontaneity, there’s a place for combativeness that doesn’t feel that feels authentic for people authentic. I’m glad you brought that word up because that’s a question I have for you. I mean, love him or hate him, people saw Trump as authentically himself in every percent, and one thing he never did is his cosplay being working class, and I think a lot of the candidates who didn’t do well on the Democratic side of the aisle would often cosplay authenticity. It’s like I’m putting on a flannel, I’m going hunting. And it was immediately I disagree. Well, I’m curious to hear, where do you see authenticity on the left side of the aisle being done well, and where are your concerns that maybe it might turn off voters who see them as being inauthentic. O.K well, first, I think Donald Trump did cosplay being working class because he put on his construction hat. And during successful campaigns I build things, I know he still had his suit on. He still had a suit on. But he’s like none of these people know how to talk to the working class. I’m from New York. I listen to that guy my whole life. I’ve heard that. And he didn’t. He was unvarnished. He’s like, I’m vulgar. I talk like this. I make things I like things I like McDonald’s, I like gold, but that connects to some voters. A lot of voters like that, but that’s part of his identity as someone who grew up in construction in New York. And construction is very tied to mafia, very tied to working class, very tied to unions that were tied to the mafia. And it’s a whole world that doesn’t really exist anywhere else. Maybe in Chicago, right, where you have billionaire elites, every day talking to their construction guys. And they share this low culture that PMC people like from my class hate looked down upon. I wouldn’t it’s so cold. It’s so he’s so vulgar, seen as tacky Yeah and I And I actually think working class people hate the PMC. Hated the PMC so much, they were like, oh, they hate him for being vulgar. They would hate me too, because I like my chachkas and my Brocade drapes like him. So there was that. I think he played that very well. I don’t know that it’s being unauthentic. I think he has very vulgar tastes. And he stood by them. He didn’t try to be anything else than that. He didn’t try to be waspy. He didn’t try to be New England. So Bernie is the same way. It’s like there’s a tri-state area thing that has to do with a local accent being very disappearing, actually, which are disappearing. It’s becoming almost exotic to hear a national figure very, very tired. I can talk like this all day long. I can talk, I can talk. I’m bringing it to this podcast. I appreciate that. I don’t like to talk like this all day long, but. But I could talk like this all day long. I had to literally get rid of my New York accent when I went to college, because I realized that people were not taking me seriously if I did. So the kinds of cosplaying that you’re talking about, I think people I don’t know if you have any examples because I can’t think of anyone. Oh, yeah. I’m sorry I had to bring it up Yeah, well, but again, someone who probably, if not perhaps crowded by political consultants would have done it differently. I mean, he had a lot of other issues as well. But I think you’re pointing to something that’s really difficult for American political culture in general, and that’s to even talk about class. You lost your accent because it marked you as a different class than the people you might be with in college. So I’m curious. And authenticity, people, people pretend to add it in order to separate themselves, perhaps from their origins. Whether those origins now in an anti-elite culture, those might be wealthy origins. You don’t want to be seen as a wealthy elite. So I’m curious, where do you see this class based kind of lens helping us here in determining future of political culture. So I’m often attacked for being a professor. Very privileged. Why should I talk about the working class. I’m not assuming the voice of the working class. I’m looking at the objective material situation of American working class people, and I think it’s because of my leftist materialist commitments that I see these things as the most important thing possible. Percent of Americans don’t even vote. They don’t participate in the electoral process, partially because they’re so alienated, partially because they’re under a lot of economic stress. They don’t have time to read the newspapers. They’re raising their children. They’re trying to put food on the table. They’re not well, physically. They don’t feel part of the polity. I feel like that is a terrible tragedy. And this is my objective assessment of the situation, that the majority of Americans don’t see their interests represented by both parties. So whether or not that’s inauthentic, I don’t care. It’s objective. Well, it’s materialist and I see the class struggle. I see the PMC, my class looking down on people like that, ignoring the interests of people like that. And this. And in this election, maybe they’ve turned a corner. I feel like it’s perfectly fine to be a class traitor. Class is not an identity. It’s a relationship to the means of production. I’m a classic Marxist on this. So it’s not like I see people using working class now as an identity. Well, as a working class person, it’s like, no, a class analysis is against as we are looking at a whole picture. We’re looking at about 65 percent of Americans who are having problems putting food on the table. Let’s pause for a moment on that, because as a conservative, I would push back a little bit on that purely materialistic class, worldview. I think that Mrs. something. I think it Mrs. some of the spiritual and social crises that we’re going through. You think about even if all of the economic conditions improved for the working class, people might still experience a crisis of meaning, feelings of anxiety that the class framing really can’t capture. We hear a lot about loneliness, epidemic isolation, the fact that people are not spending as much time in each other’s companies, those things might not be solvable by fixing all the economic issues. And the trauma scripts, in part, are probably filling some of that void. So if the trauma scripts are bad for us, which I think you argue persuasively, they are what should replace them. So I feel like I agree that there’s a question of meaninglessness and isolation. I would just I think we need more infrastructural support to create better social lives. We are a secularizing society the church and the community, the local newspapers, clubs like Robert Putnam’s in description, membership and all of those things are declining. And in place of it we have the time suck of the smartphone. I feel like there should be a deep sense of commitment in creating community centers small locally based, maybe federally funded places where people can feel like they can get a good meal, they can read a book, they can see free film. Like, I really believe in cultural enrichment that comes through building out infrastructure like this. I also feel like one of the things that isolates people is not the feeling of not having any money. When I thought I saw a really interesting statistic about how we’re just entertaining less at home. Fewer dinner parties, fewer gatherings. It takes a lot of money to have to put together a dinner. And for poor people or working class people, there’s a lot of shame about the home. I live that, as in an immigrant family. And so we need like these third spaces. And here maybe I do agree that I think that there is a really important spiritual function of these third spaces, because they allow us to neither be in high stakes public venues or perfectly private venues, that a third space provides in real life space of communion with the other. That’s very difficult because when you actually have to face other people, they often disagree with you. They’re not easy to handle. It’s much easier to go on your phone and create that substitute. So I actually believe that we can provide infrastructural spaces of meaning. What a well-functioning senior center community center actually is an incredible thing to see. My parents were involved in this before they passed away in Westchester County. They were often community based spaces. There were classes. They had a really incredible social life because of the senior centers in Westchester County. I think we should go back to some of that model for people who don’t want to go to church or who aren’t comfortable with religious belief, but to have community centers that are non-commercialized social spaces. Well, this is another point, I think, of agreement on the right and the left, in that the crisis of social connection is going to force us to come up with more creative solutions. I am also a fan of third places, especially the ones that you don’t have to pay to use, and most of those, especially for younger people who don’t want to pay $12 for a coffee to sit and talk to their friends in a place that feels kind of like a WeWork. So there’s definitely a motivation for that. We might. In fact, I’m sure we disagree on it being on federal funding being the answer. Those are long standing debates, but we are still a religious country far more than many others. And churches in those communities do provide that infrastructure. What other institutions would you think besides the federal government and the churches. Would you perhaps see as a pathway to helping in that situation I’ve been thinking about this a lot recently, because I had this long debate with one of my friends about how we could actually leverage the parish system. And a secular kind of parish system where. A lot of Social Services would be integrated into one space, you could have childcare could have free meals, and not necessarily based on any particular religion. I do think public funding does come into play to commercialize these things. I think that philanthropy is very limited as a source and also the philanthropists and the NGOs. You and I probably agree with this. They all have their own agendas. I think a neutral funding source would probably be better, but maybe federal funding distributed across states that had a lot of determination about how they would spend it. Well, I’m curious then, if we because some of the reasons I’m pushing you on the crisis of meaning and the spiritual issues, is that our politics has shown a real demoralization in the sense that some of the most transcendent things. You see, political actors on both sides do is express contempt for their opponents. Empathy is seen as weakness. Where does your critique of trauma politics fit into that politics. Which I’m sad to say a lot of people enjoy consuming as entertainment and for some is almost a secular faith. You mean the contempt. The contempt. So where do you see trauma politics either exacerbating that tendency or if we abandon trauma politics, will we see less of this contempt and lack of empathy in the political space. That’s just human nature. No, no, I think that’s a really interesting question because I think that part of that contempt culture has to do with the fact that trauma culture has created theaters of false empathy. And this is where I would go back to more of a stoic assist position, where we keep empathy to the people we know in real life, or to the caring institutions that where it should be encouraged and instantiated. And we keep it out of politics. I’ll give you an example of the institutional, the failed institutionalization of empathy that I think actually produced more alienation.
